items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we have surveyed [MATH: 100] students regarding their sports preferences, asking them whether they like baseball or volleyball. The results of our survey are shown in the Venn diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0eb5cc19648067442db072c7288d1aa5]

Content:
Now, suppose that we wish to calculate the probability that a randomly selected student who likes volleyball also likes baseball. We represent this probability symbolically as
[MATH: P(\textrm{ student likes baseball } | \textrm{ student likes volleyball }).]

Content:
Said in words, we would read the above as "the probability that a student likes baseball given that they like volleyball." This type of probability is called a conditional probability. In this case, we can think of this probability as the proportion of volleyball-liking students who also like baseball.

Content:
Since we assume that the student likes volleyball, we only need to look at the area of the Venn diagram that is inside the right-hand circle.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/978b4807bfe532261b148db61801dc83]

Content:
In total, the number of students who like volleyball is
[MATH: 30+20=50.]

Content:
Of these [MATH: 50] students, only [MATH: 30] of them also like baseball. This is represented by the area where the circles [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] overlap.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/028dbfd49f11014adcc150011ab850d2]

Content:
Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected student likes baseball given that they like volleyball, is
[MATH: P(\textrm{ student likes baseball } | \textrm{ student likes volleyball }) = \dfrac{30}{50} = \dfrac35.]

sections.normalized_html:
To compute [MATH: P(B|A),] we need to ask, "what is the probability of [MATH: B] occurring given that [MATH: A] has occurred."

Since we are assuming [MATH: A] has occurred, we only consider the probabilities inside [MATH: A.]

The probability of event [MATH: A] occurring is

[MATH: P(A)=0.3+0.1=0.4.]

Now, [MATH: P(B|A)] can be interpreted as the proportion of [MATH: B] that lies inside [MATH: A,] relative to the size of [MATH: A.] So, we have

[MATH: P(B|A) = \dfrac{0.1}{0.4} = 0.25.]

sections.normalized_html: Consider the Venn diagram below. The set [MATH: T] represents all of the customers of a cafe who like tea, and [MATH: C] represents all of the customers who like coffee. Find the probability that a randomly selected customer who likes coffee also likes tea.
sections.readable_text:
Consider the Venn diagram below. The set [MATH: T] represents all of the customers of a cafe who like tea, and [MATH: C] represents all of the customers who like coffee. Find the probability that a randomly selected customer who likes coffee also likes tea.

[IMG: /graphics/36c6c4bbd81ea1fcb61c6518278b375d]

sections.normalized_html:
We wish to compute the probability that a customer likes tea given that they like coffee. Therefore, we need to compute [MATH: P(T|C).]

To compute [MATH: P(T|C),] we need to ask, "what is the probability of [MATH: T] occurring given that [MATH: C] has occurred?"

Since we are assuming that [MATH: C] has occurred, we only consider the customers inside [MATH: C.]

In total, the number of customers that lie in the set [MATH: C] is

[MATH: 21+42=63.] Of these [MATH: 63] customers, [MATH: 21] lie inside [MATH: T.]

Since each outcome is equally likely, [MATH: P(T|C)] can be interpreted as the proportion of [MATH: T] that lies inside [MATH: C,] relative to the size of [MATH: C.] Therefore, we have

[MATH: P(T|C) = \dfrac{21}{63} = \dfrac13.]
